Log-linear conductance model

Source: R/radish_conductance_model.R
loglinear_conductance.Rd

Returns a function of class "terradish_conductance_model" that represents a log-linear mapping from spatial covariates to conductance. This is the recommended conductance model for most applications.

Usage

loglinear_conductance(formula, x)

Arguments

formula

Model formula describing which spatial covariates drive conductance. The left-hand side is ignored; only the right-hand side terms are used (e.g. ~ altitude + forestcover).

x

Data frame of spatial covariates extracted from a conductance_surface object (typically surface$x). Every variable named on the right-hand side of formula must be a column of x.

Value

A function of class "terradish_conductance_model" that accepts a numeric vector of conductance parameters theta and returns a list with elements conductance (a vector of per-cell conductance values), confint (a function for confidence intervals), and derivative functions used internally by the optimizer.

Details

The conductance at grid cell i is:

$$C_i = \exp(\theta_1 x_{i1} + \theta_2 x_{i2} + \ldots)$$

where \(x_{ij}\) is the value of covariate \(j\) at cell \(i\) and \(\theta_j\) is the corresponding conductance parameter.

The intercept is intentionally omitted: multiplying all conductances by a common factor rescales resistance inversely, and the measurement model's resistance coefficient absorbs that factor. The absolute conductance level is therefore not identifiable.

Interpreting \(\theta\):

  • \(\theta_j > 0\): higher values of covariate \(j\) increase fitted relative conductance and tend to lower graph resistance distance, conditional on the other terms and graph domain.

  • \(\theta_j < 0\): higher values lower fitted relative conductance.

  • \(\theta_j = 0\): the fitted conductance is locally unchanged by that term, conditional on the model.

  • A one-standard-deviation increase in covariate \(j\) multiplies fitted conductance by \(\exp(\theta_j)\) when the covariate was standardized and the term is linear.

These are model-based associations, not direct estimates of movement rate, habitat suitability, or a causal landscape effect.

The exponential link guarantees strictly positive conductances for any real \(\theta\).

Categorical covariates must be stored as factor columns in x (see conductance_surface for how to encode them). They are dummy-coded using the default R contrasts via model.matrix, with one level dropped as a reference. In-formula transformations such as I(x^2) and interaction terms x * z are supported.

See also

smooth_loglinear_conductance, gaussian_smoothed_loglinear_conductance, conductance_surface, terradish

Other conductance models: gaussian_smoothed_loglinear_conductance(), smooth_loglinear_conductance(), terradish_conductance_model_factory

Examples

x <- data.frame(altitude = c(-1, 0, 1), forestcover = c(0.2, 0.6, 0.5))
model <- loglinear_conductance(~ altitude + forestcover, x)

# Evaluate at specific parameter values
fit <- model(c(altitude = 0.3, forestcover = -0.2))
fit$conductance  # per-cell conductance values
#> [1] 0.7117703 0.8869204 1.2214028

# Interaction and polynomial terms work too
x2 <- data.frame(altitude = c(-1, -0.25, 0.5, 1),
                 fc = c(0.2, 0.6, 0.5, 0.8))
model2 <- loglinear_conductance(~ altitude + I(altitude^2) + fc, x2)
